subject: arts-music
lesson_title: Synthesis and review: music theory, composition, and arranging
standards: Michigan Arts Education Standards: Music — Creating
essential_question: How do harmony and form carry feeling, and how do we compose with them deliberately?
learning_objectives: Connect music theory, composition, and arranging across the unit and assemble the evidence that shows readiness for assessment.
Communicate understanding of music theory, composition, and arranging using subject-appropriate evidence or representation.
Check, revise, or improve the work on music theory, composition, and arranging against the stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task on music theory, composition, and arranging.
The learner supplies evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.

materials: manuscript paper or accessible notation tool
instrument, voice, or keyboard — a silent or written route is always available

Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.
task_brief: Day 10 of "Music Theory, Composition, and Arranging" (unit 2, grade 10) is a synthesis on music theory, composition, and arranging. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Compose and notate an original short work with harmonic analysis and an arranging rationale. Today's work contributes to that by handling music theory, composition, and arranging at the synthesis and review stage, against the unit's wider topics of chord function and progressions, melody writing and phrasing, harmony and voice leading, and form and structure. This session produces reviewable evidence toward the unit performance task.
primary_task: Draw music theory, composition, and arranging together with the other ideas built across this unit, including melody writing and phrasing. Produce a single organised artifact — an annotated portfolio page, a comparison chart, or a mapped set of your own studies — showing how at least three of the unit's ideas relate and where each one shows up in work you actually made. Then make or analyse one short example that needs two of them at once and label which is doing what. Name the idea you are least confident about and what would settle it. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about music theory, composition, and arranging, and it belongs to "Music Theory, Composition, and Arranging", which also covers separate topics such as chord function and progressions. Close out with this check before you stop: Identify which unit evidence is strongest, which is thin, and what would strengthen it. At grade 10 the bar is independent work that justifies its approach against a named alternative you considered and rejected, with the trade-off stated concretely.

Complete the critique criteria list in this package before submitting.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
For any multi-session project, supply a written milestone plan, checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown, so executive-function load is not silently part of what is being assessed.

Adjust quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode while holding the target constant. Where the target names a specific skill, change how it is evidenced rather than substituting a different skill.

Accept typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, notated, constructed, or demonstrated responses. Where performance is the target, a private demonstration to one trusted adult carries the same weight as any audience, and requires no recording.
Provide adaptive instruments and grips, enlarged or braille notation, seated and standing studio access, low-odour and low-dust material substitutes, and hearing protection on request.

Where documentation quality is itself the target, document the artwork alone with no person in frame, or have an adult verify the physical work directly. Neither route requires an image of the learner, and both preserve the documentation target rather than replacing it.
task_accessibility_provisions: This task centres a visual element (music theory, composition, and arranging). Provide tactile, raised-line, or high-relief equivalents, enlarged and high-contrast print, and a verbal description route. Never make colour discrimination alone carry a criterion — pair any colour judgement with value, label, or texture.

This work spans sessions, so supply a written milestone plan, explicit checkpoint dates, and a task breakdown. Executive-function load — sequencing, holding the plan in mind, remembering where the work stopped — must not become a silent part of what is being assessed.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Public performance is never required. A private, low-audience, or written-and-scored alternative always carries the same academic target.
No recording of the learner’s voice, no photograph, and no video is ever required; documentation may be written, notated, sketched, or adult-verified instead.
Use only original, public-domain, licensed, or family-approved works. Do not reproduce full copyrighted lyrics, sheet music, or other protected works without documented rights.
The tutor may explain technique, ask diagnostic questions, and critique work, but never silently completes graded creative work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, score excerpt, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting music theory, composition, and arranging.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile or concrete model, or adult demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for music theory, composition, and arranging follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for music theory, composition, and arranging, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to music theory, composition, and arranging works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of music theory, composition, and arranging, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking music theory, composition, and arranging mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply music theory, composition, and arranging under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on music theory, composition, and arranging rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
